summary:
Honduras is among the most dangerous countries in the Americas for trans women. Human Rights Watch finds that states in the region exclude transgender women from their femicide legal frameworks, with officials in one neighbouring jurisdiction justifying the exclusion on the ground that trans women are 'not biological women'. Vicky Hernández v. Honduras, heard by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case worldwide.

The Court's 2021 judgment held the Honduran state responsible for the 2009 killing of trans activist Vicky Hernández and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime, and ordered reforms including legal gender recognition. Implementation to date is partial.

Nothing in Honduran law criminalises being trans, and a legal name-change process exists. Against that, Human Rights Watch's 2009 report Not Worth a Penny documents police rape, assault and extortion of trans people, and the US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among the country's significant human-rights issues.

Impunity is the mechanism that sustains the violence. The LAWG Education Fund report Left in the Dark places Honduras among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, notes that trans women face the greatest obstacles to justice, and attributes the resulting impunity to under-reporting, absent police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases; the report finds that institutions 'fail to effectively investigate and prosecute'.

Placement in custody runs by birth sex. Trans women are held within the men's prison system. Human Rights Watch reported in 2020 that a Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, that she informed prosecutors, and that they did not investigate; the judge's conclusion was that 'there's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons'. Corresponsales Clave documented the same placement rule at national penitentiaries, with forced haircutting, confiscation of women's clothing, denial of conjugal visits and no policy for placement by gender identity.

Anti-discrimination provisions exist on paper. Penal Code Article 321-A (Decree No. 23-2013) punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000; Article 27 makes hatred or contempt on those grounds an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility; Article 321 punishes arbitrary denial of rights or refusal of professional service on the same grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages. The amended Penal Code took effect in March 2017 and the anti-discrimination articles were retained after lobbying by LGBTQ rights groups.

Public space is policed through a morals provision. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs allows police to raid streets, entrap sex workers under 'sanitation control' and arrest anyone who 'goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals'. LGBTQ organisations document that officers use it as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space.

Trans visibility carries a measurable security cost. A trans activist and co-founder of Asociación Cozumel Trans ran for Congress in Francisco Morazán for the 26 November 2017 election, potentially as the first openly trans officeholder, following a 2017 primary win by Kendra Stefani Jordany and Claudia Spellman's 2012 run; Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa.
tangentialFactors:
The 2005 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage and de facto unions (Article 112) and prohibiting same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116) forms part of the same conservative legislative climate in which trans rights are contested, and shows the direction of formal law on family recognition.

Religious institutions are a consistent source of pressure on policy. The Catholic Church, Pentecostals and conservative legislators organised against formal recognition of three LGBTQ rights groups in 2004; the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association called the name-change procedure for LGBTI persons an 'aberration in God's eyes'; President Juan Orlando Hernández stated on 12 October 2018 that he personally opposed same-sex marriage; and the same pastors' association later urged President Xiomara Castro to stop 'immoral laws'.

Political parties have largely kept distance from the issue. The two major parties have mostly ignored LGBTQ rights, only a handful of dissident members of the Democratic Unification Party engaged with the LGBT community, and three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats. Candidate registration itself was obstructed for LGBTQ groups from the 1980s onward.

The violence timeline runs continuously across the archived record: an August 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups, 2009–10 reporting on an LGBT activist murdered amid violence and impunity, and 2009–11 items on extreme violence against the gay community and post-coup abuses. Pride mobilisation is visible too, with about 400 people marching in San Pedro Sula in July 2017.

Regional context matters: Central America's LGBT people have been reported as fleeing their home countries for their lives, and the same regional pattern of femicide-law exclusion applies across several states.
localsOnly:
Trans women in the national penitentiaries are held in the men's system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the 'La Isla' module beside the unit for mentally ill prisoners; officers state that trans women are men and force them to cut their hair and stop presenting as women, and conjugal visits are refused. At Penitenciaria de Marcala, authorities seized one trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after CPTRT intervention was she isolated from men and her belongings returned. Placement follows birth sex, with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad-hoc protective isolation, and no placement-by-gender-identity policy.

A name change for LGBTI persons is approved, but no procedure details are published; the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association publicly denounced the procedure.

Under the Constitution, citizens may establish and associate with political parties and interest groups, though initial attempts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays. The first organisations arose in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic, held no legal standing and were largely ignored by the government apart from police harassment. In 2004 the government extended formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups despite organised protests.

The government offers medical care to all citizens and has increasingly worked with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, but the influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant churches has blocked comprehensive public programmes. Female prostitutes and men who have sex with men are identified as the highest-risk groups.

Same-sex unions are not legally recognised, and same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households do not receive the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Enforcement exposure for trans women sits largely in the 2001 modesty provision and in the Penal Code's discrimination articles, the latter carrying three to five years' imprisonment plus fines.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Reuters feature on Central America's LGBT people returned HTTP 401 and could not be retrieved at research time; the claim above rests on its indexed summary rather than the article text.

No procedure details for the legal name-change process are given in any source reviewed; the existence of approval is stated, the steps, timeline and documentation requirements are unresolved.

No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear in the sources reviewed; that gap is unresolved rather than confirmed as absent.

It is unresolved how much of the 2009 Not Worth a Penny documentation of police rape, assault and extortion still describes routine practice; the later evidence from 2017, 2020 and 2021 corroborates continuing abuse and impunity but no source in this inventory re-surveys the full pattern.

Whether the Inter-American Court's 2021 orders on legal gender recognition have been enacted in legislation is stated only as partial implementation; the specific legislative instruments outstanding are not sourced here.
